sources.title: Light · model and scientific references
sources.text:
# Afterlight · Light you can predict and use

For an ideal point lamp above a horizontal detector, E = I*h/(dx²+dy²+h²)^(3/2). Directly below the lamp, E = I/h². Contributions from independent clear lamps add. Opaque vertical screens block a ray that intersects at or below their top.

Calculated lux and separately recorded real readings are different evidence. Comparing arrangements requires the same surface and labelled point coordinates. A personal target is a chosen design goal, not a lighting standard. Candela is intensity, not electrical watts.

The model excludes ambient light, reflection, diffraction, finite fixture size and spectral changes. Point uniformity only covers the selected points. Multiple changed conditions do not isolate one cause.

Distance and the point-source model
An ideal point lamp sends light outward. On a surface facing the lamp directly, illuminance is intensity divided by distance squared: E = I / r². Keeping intensity fixed and halving the distance gives four times the illuminance. Real lamps have size and direction-dependent output, so this idealisation is most useful when the source is small relative to its distance.
Illuminating Engineering Society: https://ies.org/definitions/inverse-square-law/

Why position and angle both matter
A horizontal detector receives less illuminance when light arrives at a slant. The incidence angle is measured from the surface normal. Combining distance and angle gives E = I cos(θ) / r². In this lab cos(θ) = h/r, so a lamp contributes I h / r³. Direct contributions from independent lamps add; blocked contributions are zero.
Illuminating Engineering Society: https://www.ies.org/definitions/cosine-law/

Intensity is not electrical power
Candela describes luminous intensity in a direction. Lux describes illuminance arriving at a surface. This lab uses candela for each ideal isotropic point lamp and lux for the horizontal detectors. Adding the lamps’ intensity settings creates a puzzle budget; it does not measure watts, electricity use, perceived comfort, or compliance with a lighting standard.
National Institute of Standards and Technology: https://www.nist.gov/pml/sensor-science/optical-radiation/realization-candela

Trace the path before increasing the lamp
Geometric optics traces straight light paths in a uniform medium. Our opaque screen occupies a vertical segment from the desk to its stated height. A direct path is blocked when it meets that segment at or below the screen top. Raising intensity cannot restore a completely blocked direct path. Real scenes can receive scattered or reflected light, which this deliberately simple model excludes.
OpenStax, University Physics Volume 3: https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-3/pages/1-1-the-propagation-of-light

Afterlight · Example · A shared table
Explicit example/template study
Task: Compare light at two work points on a shared table.
Question: Which arrangement meets the point targets, and what should I check in reality?
Owner: project-959b0941-1b2d-4331-83a5-301d59998f50
Model: point-light-1
Targets revision 1: 150–200 lx; selected-point uniformity ≥ 0.9; enabled intensity ceiling not set
Chosen arrangement: Option C · equal lamps
Reason: Both selected reading places calculate 183.82 lx within my example 150–200 lx range. Equal 40 cd lamps raise the darker place without leaving the brighter place above the maximum. The model uses 80 cd total; this is not an electrical-power estimate.
Next check: Measure both reading places with the actual lamps and record the meter, time and ambient conditions.

Experiment experiment-22fca04a-8a40-4564-8503-9285f9bf0704 (2026-10-11T15:27:55.872Z)
Prediction: decrease
Original hypothesis: Raise Lamp 1 from 0.50 m to 0.70 m, keeping 40 cd and the same two points. At the point directly below it, I expect its inverse-square contribution to fall.
Conclusion: Raising only Lamp 1 from 0.50 to 0.70 m lowered the reading directly beneath it from 183.82 to 105.45 lx. Its own contribution follows I/h² while Lamp 2 remains unchanged. The larger height fails this example point target. I would check an actual extended fixture with ambient light before choosing its real placement.

studies.title: Bring the light closer
studies.task: Keep the 32 cd lamp directly above the centre detector. Change its height to reach 180–220 lx.

experiments.hypothesis: Halve the overhead height from 0.8 to 0.4 m at 32 cd. I expect four times the centre illuminance from E=I/h².
experiments.note: The centre increased from 50 to 200 lx. At fixed intensity directly below a point lamp, halving height gives four times the illumination. This does not describe a reflected or extended-source room.
experiments.explanation: Centre: 50.00 → 200.00 lx (increase). One control changed, giving a matched comparison. Each clear lamp contributes I h / r³; blocked direct contributions are zero.

experiments.hypothesis: Doubling the height from 0.4 to 0.8 m at fixed 32 cd should quarter the overhead reading.
experiments.note: 200 to 50 is one quarter. Check actual lamps next.
experiments.explanation: Centre: 200.00 → 50.00 lx (decrease). One control changed, giving a matched comparison. Each clear lamp contributes I h / r³; blocked direct contributions are zero.
